title: DfE Decoded #168: Parents Can Now Compare Schools More Easily, So Leaders Need to See What They See
author: Paul Urry
summary: Urry argues that the DfE's new Find and Compare Schools and Colleges service changes who school data is for, so every leader should look at their own school's profile as a prospective parent would. National datasets on attendance, attainment and provision now form parents' first impression, before they meet the school's own culture, curriculum or community. He argues that school websites matter more, not less, because they must supply the story and meaning behind the numbers, especially on SEND, enrichment and ethos. He warns against counting clubs rather than equitable participation and against gaming the profile. He recommends a simple audit: check accuracy, ask an outsider to explore the school online, then leave it alone with no new action plan.
points: Easier comparison means national data, including attendance and soon inspection and enrichment information, will frame parents' first impression of a school.
Websites must now provide the context the profile cannot, with SEND pages written for families rather than compliance.
Enrichment listings invite shallow counting; who participates and whether it is equitable matter more than the number of clubs.
Leaders should audit accuracy and outsider impressions but not redesign the school around the profile.
quotes: The national profile gives information. Our own communication gives meaning.
But increasingly, some of the first information a prospective parent sees will not be written by us. It will be assembled from national datasets.
A long list of clubs is easy to publish. Equitable participation is much harder to achieve.
Attendance used to feel primarily like an internal school improvement measure. Now it is increasingly becoming something parents can readily see when comparing schools.
We should not confuse easier comparison with completely free choice.
The profile should reflect the school. The school should not exist to improve the profile.
